Messages.Author: Juggernaut1981
Messages.Body:
Okay, with the several hundred posts scattered across about 4 threads
on "contesting"... it seems like people secretly have an issue with
the Transfers Rules. LSJ has made some points on it, and I thought it
might be good to get a clear space for discussing changes to the
TRANSFER RULES instead of whinging about "is contesting good/bad/ugly/
shiny".
Objective:
Create a rule to negate the scenario of you "wasting many turns and
pool and transfers to get boned cross-table cause someone influences
out your vampire".

Rule Option 1: From LSJ
>Expose a crypt card that would contest a unique card controlled by
>another player to remove that card from the game and redistribute the
>blood counters on that card among your other uncontrolled minions
>and/or your pool.

Rule Option 2:
[Insert into rules on Transfer Phase Actions]
During your transfer phase, you may spend 4 transfers and reveal a
unique card in your uncontrolled region that is currently controlled
or being contested by at least one other Methuselah. The card you
reveal is removed from the game and you may move any blood counters on
that unique card to another unique card in your uncontrolled region.

Rule Option 3:
You may spend 1 transfer to move 1 blood between two cards in your
uncontrolled region.

Since this really isn't about "contesting itself" but instead a
weakness in the Transfers system highlighted by contestation... If you
agree with one of the options, let it be known... if you have issues
with any of them debate (as I have no doubt you will)

Messages.Author: Juggernaut1981
Messages.Body:
Okay, the point is this (and has been covered EXTENSIVELY in other
threads):
Being in the situation where two people are influencing out the same
medium-to-large-vampire and someone beats you to it (especially when
it was your first minion) screws up games. Therefore, to improve the
game (and help tables not be horridly destroyed by a series of
coincidences, chance events and player decisions) a change should
potentially be made to the TRANSFER rules to reduce the TABLE-
destroying results of those coincidences, chance events and player
decisions.

So what this thread is about is:
Which Option do you like best?
Which option solves the issues, as described above (and WE DON'T need
more analysis of the issues!!!!), and doesn't create a whole raft of
other rogue-effects that will overbalance the game?

There have also been LONG discussions about the types of choices that
could be made and are summarised basically as:

Category 1: Burn the "card which would be contested" and move all pool
counters to other uncontrolled vampires and/or pool.
Category 2: Increase the speed of transferring off contested minions
(say 1TP = 1 pool back for contested or "would be contested" cards)
Category 3: Have a cup of cement princess and harden up. (No Change at
all)

CATEGORY 1:

From LSJ
>Expose a crypt card that would contest a unique card controlled by
>another player to remove that card from the game and redistribute the
>blood counters on that card among your other uncontrolled minions
>and/or your pool.

My own variation (with slightly increased cost, restricting it to
crypt-cards and reducing the places pool could be sent to)

During your transfer phase, you may spend 4 transfers and reveal a
unique card in your uncontrolled region that is currently controlled
or being contested by at least one other Methuselah. The card you
reveal is removed from the game and you may move any blood counters
on
that unique card to another unique card in your uncontrolled region.

CATEGORY 2:
#1
(From another thread, I've forgotten which and there are a few
variations on those)
1 TP = Move 1 pool to crypt card, move 1 pool from crypt card to pool
2 TP = move 1 blood from ready vampire to pool, move 1 pool to ready
vampire

#2

You may spend 1 transfer to move 1 blood between two cards in your
uncontrolled region.

CATEGORY 3: Lots of people. It's basically Current Rules, No change,
play better and harden up.

Peter Bakija... I'd love to hear your feedback since it was your rant
that started this whole thing off.

Playtesting option for those who are interested: Force the
situaiton. On a table of 5 there should be 2 pairs of 2 players
playing EXACTLY the same deck. (i.e. 5play table = 2x AAA-Toreador,
2x Obf Ven Vote, 1x Dom-Gangrel) and play with the contesting rule of
your choice. That should push up the chances of contesting and also
allow you to see how it affects people's games vs the current rule.

Messages.Author: Eek
Messages.Body:
First off I have missed this whole conversation. (Thanks for the
recaps). I have given it some though, and to achieve minimal screwing,
and manipulation of the rules the below is quite close in my opinion.

> My own variation (with slightly increased cost, restricting it to
> crypt-cards and reducing the places pool could be sent to)
> During your transfer phase, you may spend 4 transfers and reveal a
> unique card in your uncontrolled region that is currently controlled
> or being contested by at least one other Methuselah.  The card you
> reveal is removed from the game and you may move any blood counters
> on
> that unique card to another unique card in your uncontrolled region.

I would change it to.

During your transfer phase, you may reveal a unique card in your
uncontrolled region with blood counter(s) that is currently controlled
or being contested by at least one other Methuselah. The card is
removed from the game. Half(rounded up) of the blood on this card is
moved to another vampire in your uncontroled region of the players
choice (If none are present the blood goes to the blood bank), and the
rest is moved to your pool.

This way the player who was slowest to pull out the vamp should only
lose 1 round of transfers causing minimum automatic of a player being
so far behind. Forcing half of it at worst case would be 4 blood ie
being beaten to a 9-11cap. Having it not cost transfers, and moving
half back to your pool. I'd say on average 4 blood. Let's the player
transfer the gained pool that turn. Effectively losing only 1 turn of
transfers. Also by adding half must move to your uncontrolled region
should stop any shenanigans with the system, and never harm the
intended, the slower player. He/she will always have another vampire
to move it to.

Kind of seems like a backwards way of doing it. Why not just have it
all be able to move where ever? If forced to move all back to your
pool, that's not so helpful, and could lead to a "bleed though this".
Moving it all to the uncontroled has no consequences, and could be
used to your advance. My proposed option is a slap on the wrist
compared to what normally happens.

> CATEGORY 3: Lots of people.  It's basically Current Rules, No change,
> play better and harden up.

Of course there are 1308 vampires in the game. Suck it up. We're
playing rock,paper,scissors... It happens sometimes you just can't
win. On the other hand I don't see how my proposed rule would hurt any
normal game. Only give us a better chance for a more balanced table in
a tragic situation. So yeah if the rule change can only help, I'm all
for it.

Woo 3:30 am posts! Hope it's not a stupid idea... lol

-Eric Leal

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Aug 20, 7:36 pm, Juggernaut1981 <brasscompo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Peter Bakija... I'd love to hear your feedback since it was your rant
> that started this whole thing off.

Oh, heh--I was off doing other stuff and not paying attention :-)

Well, for my money, I think the best fix is:

"If you yield contestation, burn that card and move all blood counters
on that card to your pool."

Yeah, I started this whole fray with suggestions for shared/
alternating control, which while it would be cool in theory, is just
too much of a pain in the ass and probably too rule intensive to make
it worth the effort. The above fix is completely targeted and laser
guided, and has zero impact on anything other than contestation. You
still lose control of a minion, you still pay to contest, but if you
contest a big important minion early on, you get your investment back.

LSJ's plan (which is similar, but takes away undo influence as a cost
for the fix) makes perfect sense, design wise, but I think it is
probably too far into the evolution of the game to change something
that significant (i.e. removing undo influence). Yes, I agree that
Dominate could probably take the kick in the junk, but still, that is
a really significant change to the game. That most people aren't going
to see as a reasonable change just to fix contestation. I suspect that
if the change has to come as a whole bundle that includes the removal
of undo influence, most folks will be opposed to the whole bill, even
if they agree with the fix contestation line item.

So in the end, again, I'd just like to see the nice, easy, simple, low
collateral damage kind of fix I like above (just get all the blood
back on a card you yield)--if someone brings out your huge vampire
right before you do? On your turn, you bring him out too. You both
lose control of the guy. The other guy gets to either pay a pool or
get all his blood back by yielding. If he doesn't, you get to on your
turn. You both suffer a bit (which is a reasonable penalty for
contesting). If you are both super committed to keeping the guy, you
both spend a lot of pool for nothing. If one of you is willing to suck
it up and start over, you yield and get back the pool you spent.
Strikes me as a totally reasonable change. Without unwanted side
effects.

-Peter

> CATEGORY 3: Lots of people. It's basically Current Rules, No change,

This.

Well, I mean, the "play better" admonition is cracked because the
problem doesn't really crop up due to truly incompetent play. It
could be seen as cropping up due to the loss of the metagame (i.e.
failure to predict that the vampire(s) you chose would also be
chosen by somebody else) but that doesn't really cut it as real
proof of incompetence. When it happens, it's just a calculated
risk that backfired - as they do from time to time.

All that said, the problem here is not broken enough to warrant the
kinds of risky and (IMHO) traumatic fixes that are getting kicked around.
It's been an entertaining thread with which to waste a bit of time
waiting for news of Heirs to the Blood - but let's not actually do
anything about it.

Fred

The point of not allowing it to "leave" the uncontrolled region is to

governs to my 5-cap twice, I burn them and get 6 pool for 4 transfers
and loosing a vampire i wouldn't bring out". I have far less issue

I don't think this should replace the "transfer back" rule (it has its
own place and should stay as is) this is about adding an additional
way to spend your Transfers to mitigate a scenario people think is
particularly bad, etc, etc, etc.

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
I think dynamic vampire contestation would be more interesting than
changing the transfer rules in any of these ways.

LSJ suggested it briefly in that monster thread.

**Whenever a player brings a unique vampire (or imbued, etc.) into the
controlled region that is already controlled by another player, the
iteration of the vampire currently in play is returned face down to
its owner's controlled region with all its blood and attached cards.**
(similar to Banishment)

Even if you can get back your pool and transfers with one of the rules
proposed in this thread, it doesn't mean you'll still have the chance
to use a critical vampire that someone else got out first.

Contestation is currently all or nothing. If the control went back
and forth based on who most recently influenced the vampire, it would
add strategic depth to the game when vampire contestation occurred:

Contestable vampire comes out before you can bring out your copy -->
Wait until it loses blood/make it lose blood/screw this, I don't care
if the other one's full! -->
Bring out your own copy, other copy banished to the uncontrolled
region -->
Other player decides whether to spend enough pool to fill it up again/
waits until the best moment to do so/it's already full so back it
goes! -->
Rinse and repeat.

That's more interesting AND more liberal than the current rule. It's
more interesting than "I get back all my pool and transfers with new
rule X, but I still have no real chance to use the vampire I need".

It is also true to the flavor of the game: Two Methusalehs vie for
control of a minion. The minion's allegiances change based on which
side most recently fulfilled its requirements for service, a "What
have you done for me lately?" rule, as it were. A true struggle
ensues.

me) was along the lines of "swap control of the contested minion at
the start of each of your turns", which would mean that you get to use
the guy on your turn, and your opponent got to use the guy on his turn

superstar, and you still lost the turns influencing out the guy, but
at least you get all your pool back instantly, so if there is a way to
salvage your position, you can start trying to do so.

For a scenario, this is purely exemplary and I'm not looking to say
this covers every situation but is intended to indicate a situation
where I think that getting the blood back from a minion you stop
contesting hurts the game.

MethA has Edward Vignes (3 blood) Anneke (7 blood) and 5 pool + 1VP
MethB has Jan Pieterzoon (5 blood) William Waldberg (6 blood) and has
planned to influence out Anneke to contest and will have around 5 pool
after starting the contest.

The point of the Contest is clearly to stop Anneke's ability to block
and allow Meth B to have a chance to oust their prey. Anneke has been
on the table for a considerable period of time and will have taken
actions and blocked actions that have more than counterbalanced her
initial cost (and has gained blood at various times so she has 7 blood
at the moment). Meth B is taking a big gamble that their predator
will not manage to oust them while they still continue the contest of
Anneke.

Using the "Yield and gain their current blood" rule:
If Meth A concedes the contest immediately, they have effectively
gained 7 pool (more than you gain for ousting and it is not blockable
by anyone and cannot be janked around by DI/Wash/Sudden/Bleeding the
Vine) because they've been able to prevent 10 pool loss and take
forward actions to gain 6 pool from ousting.

It is in Meth As interest to hold the contest for as long as possible
because Meth B has more to gain by yielding than they do by contesting
(10 immediate pool gain as opposed to 6 from ousting implying a net
difference of -1 per turn of contest which is at most 4 turns).

Using the current rules
It is in Meth Bs interest to hold the contest for as long as possible,
since they have 6 pool to gain from their prey and will have wasted 10
pool to get it (net pool loss of 4 + pool used to maintain contest)
unless they win the contest. It is actually in Meth As interest to
yield the contest to minimise their ongoing pool damage UNLESS they
have a guaranteed way to generate 1 pool per turn.

Messages.Author: Legendre
Messages.Body:
Here's what you said. I'll let it speak for itself:

"There is no fun.

There is only thousands of dollars wasted on a trip to sit with your
thumb up your butt for 30 minutes while you're ousted. "

My point was not to make a personal attack, but was directed at your
method of argument. I actually sincerely doubted that you really
believe that your thousands of dollars were "wasted" -- I think you're
just trying to make a slightly disingenuous rhetorical point.
Perhaps you were serious after all, though, given your statement that
the focus of the rules should be on competition and not fun.

Here's what I see as the real root of the problem: When the game
first came out, contesting happened all the time. Elder Library, Mob
Connections, The Elysium, vampires like Gideon Fontaine, Aleph, Didi
Meyers, and Sir Walter Nash, the Ivory Bow, and even Thaddeus Zho got
contested on a fairly regular basis because there weren't that many
unique cards.

But with every expansion, players' expectations of contesting have
gotten lower and lower. Every new vampire added to the mix means a
smaller likelihood of someone running your exact deck. The grouping
rules make it even LESS likely that you'll contest. With hundreds of
vampires to choose from, contesting happens far more rarely. (The
exception to this trend consists of cards that are good in pretty much
every and any deck type: Van Wyk, Heart of N., the Barrens, etc. But
vampires - with the possible exception of Ian Forestal - are not of
this genus.)

Now, with many many expansions behind us, what used to be an integral
part of the game starts to seem like an outlying annoyance, or even a
penalty incurred through no fault of our own. Decks aren't built with
contesting in mind because, more often than not, it's simply not an
issue. When was the last time you saw a Praxis: Solomon played? I
stopped including them in my decks after Final Nights. There hasn't
been one in a TWD since 2005. But just because people have, as a
matter of habit, stopped preparing (both psychologically and in deck
construction) for a situation does not mean on that basis alone that
we should get rid of the rules that give rise to that situation.

I think that the wide variety of cards available to us, and the
lowered expectations of contesting, should not blind us to the thrill
of slapping down a vampire that's already out, narrowing our eyes, and
daring our opponent to keep paying pool, or, alternatively, to
engaging in table diplomacy as we quickly reallocate our resources and
pray. Those of us who have been playing since the game came out used
to know these things -- we *must* have or we wouldn't have kept
playing all these years.

Or...

..or perhaps the point *is* competition and not fun. Perhaps the
greater variety of cards has just led to faster, more efficient decks
-- much like the Magic decks that are able to win in their first turn
-- that no longer really admit of an opportunity to enjoy contesting.
If that's what's going on, then the game is becoming less about play
and more about mechanics. (Hence my earlier comment about deciding
the game by algorithm instead of playing.) That's certainly what
sucked the fun out of Magic for me and got me to limit my card-game
playing to Jyhad exclusively -- it became impossible to just find a
relaxed, fun game of Magic. People stopped thinking about what the
cards depicted and focused solely on what the cards did in a
functional sense, and cards became less about modeling some fictional
struggle or conflict and more about establishing mathematical
relationships among the cards and recursions and such. And, now that
I'm thinking about it, that would explain how we get something like
the Heart of Nizchetus, which increases a deck's mechanical efficiency
but leaves one wondering exactly why *that* particular card has *that*
particular effect. (Summon Soul, by contrast, at least has the patina
of pulling spirits with ancient knowledge from the afterworld and
priming them for action.)

So maybe, in the end, Jeff's actually right... maybe the game's design
shouldn't focus on fun, but on competition and making sure that the
rules themselves never put someone in a really difficult position that
they didn't "deserve" in some in-that-game-decision sense. Certainly
if VTES were a betting sport rather than a card game, someone would
make a point similar to the one Jeff is making. After all, there'd be
money riding on the results so you'd want to do everything you could
to eliminate unnecessary chaos in outcomes, so as to avoid people's
"wasting" thousands of dollars.

But I'd hate to think that's what the game's becoming.

LSJ my point is this:
If you have paid for a vampire, *gained beneficial use* of that
vampire *before* someone contests it, then why should you in effect
get a *refund* on that vampire if you decide to let someone else have

that she's not playing competitively, even though she's playing as
well as she can (and does win about as much as she loses).

John Eno

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Playing as well as she can means that she's maximizing her score to the best of
her ability.

Not much, if anything, would separate that from playing competitively.
Underlying motivations notwithstanding.

When I play chess with my kids, I'm not invested in the outcome, but that is
very different than saying we don't play competively.

What would make the game less fun is if one of us decided to just play silly
(conforming to the mechanics of chess, but playing Malkavian Knights or
something) -- ignoring the victory conditions specified in the rules.

Or, at least, that would be less fun for the other person (assuming the other
person was playing with the full rules set, victory conditions included).

Okay. It seems that "competition" has a much harder-edged connotation
in my head than it does in yours. A person who lacks strong investment
in outcome, in the sense of how much effort they're willing to expend
on winning, is a person who isn't playing competitively, as far as I'm
concerned. Or to put it another way, someone who plays as well as they
can but isn't trying to play very hard isn't playing competitively.

It also occurs to me that Kevin and I may have been talking past each
other. I assumed he was talking about games in terms of the process of
playing games; he may very well have meant games in the sense of a set
of rules and components. In which case I agree with him that there are
few if any non-competitive games.

John Eno

Howdy,

> It also occurs to me that Kevin and I may have been talking past each

> playing games; he may very well have meant games in the sense of a set
> of rules and components. In which case I agree with him that there are

Thinking about it a bit myself, it seems to me that most 'games' that
are seemingly non-competitive (solitaires of various stripes,
collaborative games [e.g. Arkham Horror], etc.) are probably more
properly termed 'puzzles', in the sense that you're trying to 'solve'
them, rather than 'play' them. You can always turn a puzzle into a
competition, though, by finding some method of scoring it (time to
complete, optimality/efficiency of solution, etc.).

Hope that helps,
Alex

Messages.Author: Legendre
Messages.Body:
There are many games that have "winners" but which have no real
competition except maybe inside people's heads:

Candyland.
Roulette.
War (the card game with a standard 52-card deck)

On the other extreme, there are games like chess and other games of
zero chance/perfect information. Those games are pure competition:
the whole point is that it's a measure of the players' skill at the
game.

Then there's Tag -- a game with no winner, ever. It doesn't stop
until people get tired of it. It's still a competition, but the
"winning" (if you want to call it that) is so transient that it really
does just sort of fade away into the play.

Now let's talk about VTES.

VTES is somewhere between Candyland and Chess. People want
"competition"... and from what I've read here, that means that people
want the game to be a test between players that somehow reflects their
skill. But it's also got huge elements of random chance in it. Think
about the way people like Lasombra are talking about this contesting
issue... the complaint is that somehow having to contest a big vampire
is a matter of chance. It's something "bad" that happens to you that
you don't deserve.

On that basis, the argument goes, we should amend the rules so that
VTES is more like chess and less like Candyland.

But people also don't deserve to have all of their master cards on the
bottom of their deck, either. The most perfectly designed deck in the
world can still run into that problem -- and will. Now, Magic has
decided that the way to deal with that is the Paris/Mulligan system.
The idea is to steepen the card-distribution curve, reducing the
extreme ends of "all land" and "no land" and swell up that nice fat
middle part where you get a good balance if your deck is constructed
soundly.

More like chess. Less like Candyland.

A lot of poker players I know *hate* no-limit five card draw. They
prefer Texas Hold 'em. Now, some of them just prefer it because it's
popular and on TV and such. But some of them prefer it because it has
more information -- you don't get absolutely blindsided by someone's
full house. You at least know when it's more and less likely.

Does that mean that Texas Hold 'em is more *competitive* than No-Limit
Five Card Draw? I can't see that that's true. Mike Caro loved his
Five Card draw, and no one would say he wasn't a competitive card
player. A lot of players I know like the game, too, and several of us
prefer it, considering it a much purer form of poker: a game where
there's less in the cards and more in the psychology.

But I digress. Back to VTES.

VTES is "competitive" in a way that tag isn't because there's a
winner. The question that we need to ask ourselves is, "What is it
that we want winning to be representative of?" If winning is
representative of pure skill in deck building, then people should not
be allowed to play a deck that they didn't design. That's clearly NOT
what we want. We don't care if someone comes to a tournament with
someone else's deck. They get less bragging rights, perhaps, but they
still win if they win.

If we want winning to be representative of pure "playing" then we need
to radically redesign the game to make it into a game of perfect
information and eliminate the random elements. Since the whole game
is premised on drawing unknown cards from a randomly shuffled deck,
that might be hard to do.

So obviously, then, we are going to have to accept a certain amount of
Candyland in our Chess. "Winning" is going to be representative of a
mixture of good luck and good play. The question then becomes where
we want the balance to be. To shift things more towards Chess, we
can have rules like:

* You get your pool back when you yield a minion in a contest.
* You get to shuffle your master card deck separately and then you get
to choose which library you draw from depending on whether you judge
that you need a master card or not. (I seem to recall seeing this
variant on one of the boards somewhere.)
* A neutral representative goes through your deck at the start of the
tournament and gives you as close to a perfectly entropic distribution
of cards as possible, dispersing clumps.
* Everyone declares their deck type at the beginning of the tournament
and we program the Archon to avoid sitting someone between two
dedicated combat wall decks.
* Everyone plays with an open hand. All the time.

If we want to move things more towards the Candyland model instead, we
can:

* Have the Edge be a six-sided die that you roll to determine whether
you gain 1, 2, or 3 pool.
* Pick one person at each table to be the Scumpot, and another to be
the Blessedprettylight. The Scumpot starts with 5 less pool, but gets
to put two master cards in play at the beginning of the game and all
his minions get +1 stealth. THe Blessedprettylight's minions can all
take actions to burn a vampire.
* Everyone picks their crypt, and brings 50 library cards. At a
particular table, everyone's library is combined into one central
library from which everyone draws. Everyone gets one additional
discard phase action. The ash heap is communal, too.

The point is just this: when people say that they want "Competition"
what they *usually* mean is that they'd like the winning of the game
to be representative of a greater degree of skill, and less a matter
of random chance. The idea is something like "a Competition is
something that you can TRY to win". You can't *try* to win
Candyland. You can only play it. I personally think this is a poor
definition of competition, but that's neither here nor there.

But two things, I think, should be kept in mind: (1) VTES has huge
elements of random chance built structurally into it (not even
counting the Malk cards) and that's one of the reason that most of its
players like to play it; (2) Contesting ISN'T ACTUALLY an entirely
random thing, at least on a macro scale. People have a decent idea of
what types of decks are going to be contested more and less often, and
the fact that some deck types are played more often and thus run a
higher risk of being contested is a *check* on their power. It helps
maintain game balance in the long run by encouraging people to play a
wider variety of decks.
